question: Why is a leaf green?
teaser: Go from an oak tree into one of its leaves and the molecule that gives the colour, then find out which colours it takes in and what happens to the green.

stops.title: An English oak
text: An oak is covered in leaves: this model draws about 9,500, and a real tree has more. Each leaf is a thin, flat sheet that catches light, a little like a solar panel, and a small chemical factory. It takes in light, water and carbon dioxide and makes sugar for the whole tree.
stops.model: A procedural model of a typical English oak, not a scan of one real tree.
stops.notice: Look at how the leaves are spread out so that most of them catch light.

stops.title: One leaf
text: An oak leaf is about 10 to 12 centimetres long, with rounded lobes along its sides. Its flat shape gives it a large surface for catching light.
The green colour comes from a molecule called chlorophyll. To see where it sits, we have to look inside.
stops.notice: Find one lobed leaf among the branches, click it, and choose "Look inside the leaf" on its card.

stops.title: Inside the leaf
text: Cut across, a leaf is only a fraction of a millimetre thick. Under the top skin stand rows of tall cells packed like fence posts, called the palisade layer, crowded with green parts called chloroplasts. Below them is a looser layer with air gaps, and pores called stomata on the underside let carbon dioxide in.
stops.model: An illustration of the layers of a typical broadleaf leaf, not a micrograph of an oak leaf. The layer thicknesses and the number of chloroplasts per cell are simplified.
stops.notice: Click a tall palisade cell. The small green discs inside are chloroplasts.

stops.title: A plant cell and its chloroplasts
text: A palisade cell holds many dozens of chloroplasts, up to about 100 in some plants. A chloroplast is a small compartment where light is turned into chemical energy.
The big empty-looking space in a plant cell is a water-filled vacuole, and the stiff cell wall keeps the shape.
stops.model: Schematic: sizes are right overall, but there are far fewer parts than a real cell has.
stops.notice: Find the chloroplasts and click one.

stops.title: The green molecule
text: This is chlorophyll a. A flat ring of carbon and nitrogen atoms holds a single magnesium atom at its centre, and a long tail anchors it in the chloroplast's membrane.
The ring is what catches light, and its structure decides which colours of light it takes in and which it lets by.
stops.model: A ball-and-stick picture of one molecule. Bond lengths are true, but the atoms are drawn smaller than their real size so that the bonds show, and the colours are a convention, not real colours.
stops.notice: Look for the single magnesium atom in the middle of the ring.

stops.title: Which colours it takes in
text: Sunlight is a mixture of colours, and each colour is a different wavelength of light, from about 400 nanometres (violet) to about 700 (red). Chlorophyll a takes in blue light most strongly, with a peak near 430 nanometres, and red light, with a peak near 660, measured in a solvent. In between, in the green, it takes in light much more weakly.
stops.notice: Look at the grass and the trees. Their green is the colour their chlorophyll takes in least.

stops.title: What happens to the green
text: Weakly does not mean not at all. In one study of lettuce leaves, a leaf took in about 93 percent of blue light, 92 percent of red light and 81 percent of green light from LEDs. The rest bounces off cell walls and air gaps or passes through, and what bounces back out of the top is the light you see.
The green that is taken in is used: in strong white light, green drove photosynthesis in sunflower leaves more efficiently than red, because it reaches deeper chloroplasts.
stops.model: An illustration of the layers of a typical broadleaf leaf, not a micrograph of an oak leaf. The percentages come from lettuce, not oak.
stops.notice: A leaf looks green because green is the colour it absorbs least, not because it ignores green.

answer: A leaf looks green because chlorophyll takes in red and blue light much more strongly than green, so the light that bounces back to your eyes is richest in green. A leaf still takes in most of the green light that reaches it, and uses it.
unknown: The colour itself is well understood. Why plants use a pigment that takes in green weakly, rather than one that takes in all colours, is still debated.
sources: Chlorophyll a peaks 428 and 660 nm in diethyl ether: Bjorn, Papageorgiou, Blankenship, Govindjee 2009, Photosynthesis Research 99:85-98 (https://www.life.illinois.edu/govindjee/Bjorn_et_al%282009%29PRES99_85-98.pdf)

Absorptance of lettuce leaf, blue 93.2 percent, green 81.1 percent, red 91.6 percent (LED-weighted), minimum 69.8 percent at 500 to 551 nm in one leaf spectrum; 'Green light is least absorbed by green leaves': Liu and van Iersel 2021, Frontiers in Plant Science 12:619987 (https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpls.2021.619987/full)

Green light drives photosynthesis more efficiently than red in strong white light, in sunflower: Terashima et al. 2009, Plant and Cell Physiology 50:684-697, doi 10.1093/pcp/pcp034 (abstract and summaries read)
